prize_parts.citation: for their theory of credit cycles, showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic shocks

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a specific, general-equilibrium mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values link asset prices to investment and output, so a small shock to net worth is amplified and persists over time. This is a distinct discovery rather than a refinement of an earlier one. It is the conceptual base for much of the later macro-finance literature on financial frictions, balance-sheet channels and crisis dynamics, and it is used in both academic and policy-oriented quantitative models. Attribution is the cleanest of any shortlisted macro candidate: the founding paper has two authors and the mechanism is theirs. The work is about three decades old and has been tested, extended and criticised over that time, so maturity is not a concern. Having re-read my own and my colleagues' rankings, I still judge this to be the most clearly bounded and foundational contribution on the list. The ballot also credits Gertler and Gilchrist, but their financial-accelerator and empirical strand is a separate, if related, contribution. Excluding them keeps the citation about one idea.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial thematic overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which could make the Committee see the field as covered. A second concern is that the evidence for the mechanism is mostly indirect. The theory is clean, but identifying the collateral channel in micro data is harder, and much of the confirmation comes through calibrated models. Only a minority of members rank this ballot at all, so I should check whether that reflects a scientific objection I have not heard. The objections raised so far are overlap and identification, and I treat both as real but not decisive. If the Committee concludes that the financial-accelerator tradition and Kiyotaki–Moore must be recognised together, the attribution boundary becomes harder and the case weakens.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B017 first as a coherent, field-creating programme and ranks B037 fourth. He flags possible overlap with the 2022 prize and says the empirical validation of the amplification channel is mixed.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical validation is weaker than the theory, and I list it among my own uncertainties. I disagree that this should put B037 below B017. The 2022 prize recognised the role of banks and runs in crises, and the Kiyotaki–Moore mechanism is a different channel: collateral values and asset prices drive dynamic amplification. The value of the contribution lies in the structural mechanism and its uptake in quantitative macro, not in a single clean test. I keep B017 as an alternative. I find the 2024 overlap concern less persuasive for Persson and Tabellini than for the institutions-and-growth literature, but the Besley question still needs resolving.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first, arguing that the task-based account and the China-shock evidence are empirically credible, widely replicated and policy-relevant. He also notes that Dorn is left out and that the task framework is close to Acemoglu's recognised work.
responses.response: I accept the empirical credibility and the policy reach. My difficulty is attribution. The ballot combines two separable strands, skills and tasks versus trade shocks, and any three-name selection omits a legitimate claimant. In my own opening I proposed only Autor and Hanson, which leaves out Katz and Dorn and shows how unstable the boundary is. Your point about the overlap with 2024 and with Goldin in 2023 raises a further question about the marginal case. For those reasons I keep B038 out of my preferred configuration, though I do not dismiss it. If the Committee can agree a boundary that is principled rather than a compromise, I would revisit it.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B044 first. She argues that the heterogeneous-firm framework transformed trade analysis and is now textbook material. She also names the attribution gap around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the Krugman 2008 prize as a possible reason for reduced appetite.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz (2003) is a major, mature contribution, and I ranked B044 third myself. I do not think the Krugman prize disqualifies it, since heterogeneous firms and selection are a distinct advance on the earlier trade theory. The attribution gap you raise is the point that keeps me from placing it first. The empirical foundations of exporter selection were laid partly by people not on this ballot, and I cannot resolve that from the supplied evidence. I therefore list B044 as my first alternative, not as a second prize part.

responses.point: Strömberg also ranks B037 first. He argues for restricting the award to the two originators, Kiyotaki and Moore, because Gertler and Gilchrist belong mainly to the related financial-accelerator line.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name restriction, for the same reason of keeping the citation to a single idea. I would qualify one point. Gertler's wider record is also tied to the New Keynesian ballot B025, so his role is not exclusive to the financial-accelerator line, and the Committee should not assume he is excluded cleanly. Like you, I have not verified the boundary between the Kiyotaki–Moore and Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist contributions beyond my own knowledge. Convergence on this ballot among a few members is not itself scientific evidence, so I rest the case on the mechanism and attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the collateral-constraint mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the work recognised in 2022, which I have not checked against the 2022 scientific background.
Whether Gertler and Gilchrist should be credited, and where the boundary lies between the Kiyotaki–Moore mechanism and the financial-accelerator tradition.
How much weight the largely model-based and indirect empirical support for the amplification channel should carry.
For B044, whether the missing empirical pioneers (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) make a clean two-person credit impossible.
For B038, whether a principled three-name boundary exists given the Autor, Katz, Hanson and Dorn strands and the adjacent 2023 and 2024 prizes.
I have not independently verified citation or impact figures.
statement.conflict_note: The profile documents no connection to Kiyotaki or Moore. I am an IIES colleague and frequent co-author of committee colleagues Krusell and Boppart (and a co-author with Friberg), so I disclose those ties generally. None of them is on the credited names of B037. My own research is in macroeconomics, including dynamic political economy and public finance with Krusell, Storesletten, Zilibotti and Rodríguez Mora. That is field proximity to B017 and macro-finance, which I disclose and do not treat as merit. No recusal need is apparent from the supplied profile.
